title.text: Shrine of the Holy Infant Jesus of Prague (Davao)

title_en.text: Shrine of the Holy Infant Jesus of Prague (Davao)

tagline.text: A hilltop pilgrimage site of the Holy Infant on Shrine Hills, overlooking Davao

location.label: Location
location.text: Shrine Hills (the hilly stretch of Broadcast Avenue), Matina, Davao City

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: December–May dry season, January 15 feast day

children.text: This Catholic pilgrimage site sits on Shrine Hills, about a 10-minute drive from downtown Davao. It has a chapel housing the image of the Infant Jesus of Prague, a Way of the Cross, and gardens with views of the city and Davao Gulf, making it a quiet place to rest even if you are not a believer.
The Shrine of the Holy Infant Jesus of Prague is a Catholic shrine at the top of Shrine Hills in the Matina area of Davao City. Locals often simply call it Shrine Hills. It is about
4km
from the city center, roughly
10 minutes

by car, yet the moment you climb the hill the city noise fades and you find tall trees and lawns. For Davao residents it is a place to pray, and on weekends also a spot where families spread out a picnic.

The heart of the shrine is the image of the Infant Jesus of Prague. It is modeled on the statue of the Infant Jesus kept at the Carmelite monastery in Prague, Czech Republic: a crowned Child Jesus with one hand raised in blessing and the other holding a globe topped with a cross. It is known for the rich vestments that devotees have offered over the years. According to local accounts, the image arrived in Davao on January 15, 1968, and was first enshrined in a small shrine built by a family in Matina. January 15 is still the feast day each year, and the shrine is busiest around then.

The devotion to the Infant Jesus has deep roots in Europe. According to local accounts, it goes back to Saint Teresa of Avila, and the statue passed through several noble families in Spain and Prague before reaching the Carmelites of Prague in 1623. The Davao image is a replica of the one in the Prague monastery, said to have been brought from Prague by a man named Briccio Santos at his mother's urging. Knowing this history, it is fascinating to think that a small statue on a hill traveled so far to reach the southern Philippines. Devotion to the Santo Niño is widespread in the Philippines, so the Infant Jesus is an especially familiar figure for the faithful who come here.

For travelers, this is not a place to see grand architecture like a big cathedral. The way to enjoy it is to walk up slowly along the Way of the Cross, sit for a while in the chapel, and look out over Davao and the sea from the end of the garden. It fits well as a restful half-day break during sightseeing in Davao, and it pairs nicely with Davao's cathedral as a religious-sites route. Because it is a place of faith, please mind your clothing and behavior. You do not need to be Catholic to visit. Entry is free, and it is one of the few places where you can sit quietly for an hour in the middle of a busy trip. Davao is a city with big attractions such as durian, seafood, Mount Apo and Samal Island, so itineraries tend to get packed, and this shrine works as a comma in between where you can catch your breath.

blocks.title: Image of the Holy Infant of Prague

children.text: This is the core of the shrine. Visitors report that the crowned Infant Jesus, in a blessing pose, is kept inside a glass case. The vestments are changed regularly, so the image may look a little different each time you go.
Stations of the Cross line the path up to the shrine. For believers it is a path to walk in prayer, and for travelers it serves as a slow walking trail in the shade of the trees.

There are several small chapels on the grounds, and behind the administration building is a covered area for offering candles. There is a steady stream of people lighting candles and offering prayers of petition or thanks.
A statue of Saint Joseph carrying the Infant Jesus stands on the grounds. It is a popular photo spot for families.

blocks.title: Views of the city and Davao Gulf

children.text: Because it is on a hill, you get an open view down over Davao and toward Davao Gulf. On a clear afternoon, the city buildings and the sea come into view at once.

The novena to the Infant Jesus is known to be prayed hourly over nine hours in a single day. People with urgent petitions come to offer this prayer. On the feast day it continues all day together with Masses.

The gardens mix tall trees, well-kept lawns and plants such as tall cacti. Visitor reviews often mention birdsong and clean restrooms. There is also a children's playground, which makes it good for a family outing.
There is said to be a small shop selling religious items such as rosaries. Many visitors buy an Infant Jesus medal or a candle as a keepsake.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: Enjoy the shrine, gardens and views

children.text: Arrive at Shrine Hills from downtown Davao by taxi or ride-hailing car. The morning is cool and less crowded, which is good for a quiet visit.
Walk slowly up along the Way of the Cross and get used to the atmosphere of the grounds.
Sit and rest, or pray, in the chapel that houses the Infant Jesus image. If Mass is in progress, stay quietly at the back.
Offer a candle at the candle area, then look around the statue of Saint Joseph and the small chapels.
Rest at the garden viewpoint, looking down over Davao and the gulf. You can also eat snacks you brought in the resting area.
Book your ride back in advance and head down. Go into the city for lunch.

On Sunday mornings the grounds are crowded because of Mass, so if you want a quiet visit, choose a weekday morning or early afternoon. If you are traveling with children, set aside some time to rest at the playground on the grounds.

items.title: Davao religious sites half day
items.subtitle: Combine the shrine with the city cathedral

children.text: Start around the cathedral in the city. At
San Pedro Cathedral
you will meet the center of Catholic life in Davao.
Take a taxi to Shrine Hills. Walk the gardens in the late afternoon light.
If you time it for the weekday afternoon Mass, you can feel the atmosphere together with local worshippers.
Watch the city turn evening colors from the viewpoint, then head down. It is best to travel before it gets dark.
Mass times can change, so check with the shrine before you visit.
A direct flight from Manila (NAIA) to Davao International Airport (DVO) takes about
2 hours
. Several flights run each day, so you can choose one that fits your schedule.
From the airport to the city, use a taxi or ride-hailing car. Fares vary with traffic, so check in the app.

items.title: From the city to the shrine

children.text: It is about
4km
from the center of Davao, around
10 minutes
by taxi or ride-hailing car.
An older visitor account advises asking the driver to wait when you take a taxi up, because taxis can be hard to find for the trip down. A ride-hailing app is convenient.
You can also take a jeepney toward Matina, but according to visitor reviews they are infrequent and are often full.
The hill is steep, and some worshippers walk up on Sundays and during Holy Week. In the heat, a taxi is recommended.

items.title: Getting around near the feast day

children.text: On the January 15 feast day there may be road closures and crowds. In 2025 and 2026 the city traffic office (CTTMO) ran one-way traffic from Pluto Street to the ABS-CBN Compound, regulated entry at the C.P. Garcia Highway–Shrine Hills Road intersection, and no entry on Pluto Street from 3 p.m., with designated parking areas and nearby private vacant lots. This can change each year, so check the latest announcements for that year.

Davao gets fairly even rainfall all year, so the difference between dry and rainy seasons is not large, but since this is a place where you walk uphill, days with less rain are more comfortable. During the day, morning and late afternoon are good for walking, and the midday sun is strong.

The most special day is the January 15 feast day. There is a dawn procession (starting around 5 a.m. in both 2025 and 2026), a novena lasting all day and Masses (6 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with a 9 a.m. pontifical Mass led by the archbishop), and many worshippers bring their own Infant Jesus images to be blessed. Choose this day if you want to see the lively atmosphere, and a weekday morning if you want quiet.

There is no lodging at the shrine itself, so the usual plan is to stay in downtown Davao and make a round trip. Downtown has hotels in a range of price levels, and the cathedral, malls and restaurants are close, making it easy to travel to and from the shrine.

A restaurant with views is said to be near the shrine, and snack vendors sometimes set up outside the entrance. It is easier on the stomach to eat in the city and bring only water and light snacks to the shrine. Check whether it is open before you go.

Davao is famous for durian, so many travelers add a stop at a fruit stall or market to taste it after returning to the city. Durian has a season, and many hotels restrict bringing it in, so check your lodging's rules first. Downtown has many Filipino and seafood restaurants, so it is easy to have lunch or dinner after visiting the shrine.
Weekday mornings are the quietest. Avoid taking photos during Mass, and take care not to capture people who are praying.
Modest clothing that covers shoulders and knees is recommended. Take off your hat inside the chapel.
It helps to book your ride down in advance or ask the driver to wait.

For inquiries, use the shrine's official Facebook page and the phone numbers listed there.
The road is a hill, so comfortable shoes are good, and bring a hat and water at midday.
Keep some small cash handy for candles or donations.
Around the feast day, many locals bring Infant Jesus or Santo Niño images to be blessed. Even if you are only watching, stay at the edge so you do not block the line.
This is not a place to stay for long, so half a day within your Davao itinerary is enough. If you have time left, continue to a nearby restaurant with a view or to the city cathedral.
It is a place of faith. Avoid loud noise and flash photography during Mass and prayer, and prepare for road closures and crowds on the feast day.
Mass times and opening hours differ between sources, so check the official page before you visit.
Taxis may be hard to find for the ride down, so decide your transport in advance.
The hill road is awkward to travel after dark, so come down before sunset.
Keep valuables on your person, and watch for pickpockets on crowded feast days.
Phone maps may show the address differently, for example as Shrine Hills Road, so search by name.
